nameStory: Low frostweed gets its charming name from the delicate ice crystals that form around its stem base on cold autumn mornings. These frost formations look like tiny frozen flowers, creating a magical winter display that early botanists found enchanting enough to inspire the common name.
description: Low frostweed is a small, sprawling perennial wildflower that hugs close to the ground, rarely growing taller than 8-12 inches. It produces cheerful yellow flowers with five delicate petals that look like tiny roses, which is why it's also called low rockrose. This hardy little plant belongs to the rock-rose family and spreads in low mats across sandy, rocky areas where few other plants can thrive.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright yellow flowers with five papery-thin petals that feel delicate like tissue paper and crinkle easily when touched, blooming from late spring through summer

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low, spreading mats that stay close to the ground, creating dense carpets rarely exceeding one foot in height

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Small, narrow leaves arranged alternately along the stems, feeling slightly fuzzy to the touch with a grayish-green color

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Produces small, round capsules that split open when ripe to release tiny brown seeds

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Woody at the base with newer growth feeling soft and slightly hairy, often reddish-brown in color

habitat: Low frostweed thrives in sandy, well-drained soils in open areas like coastal plains, pine barrens, and rocky outcrops. It prefers full sun locations with poor, acidic soil where competition from other plants is minimal. In New England, look for it in disturbed sandy areas, old fields, and along woodland edges with sandy substrate.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as small grayish-green shoots from woody base stems. Early leaves appear fuzzy and soft to the touch.
seasonality.summer: Bright yellow flowers bloom from June through August, opening in the morning sun and often closing by afternoon on hot days.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and seed capsules ripen, splitting open to release seeds. This is when the famous frost formations appear around stem bases on cold mornings.
seasonality.winter: Above-ground portions die back, but woody base remains visible. The fascinating ice crystal formations continue to appear during freeze-thaw cycles.

funFact: Low frostweed creates its own natural ice sculptures by forcing moisture up through its stems on freezing nights, creating ribbon-like ice formations that can be several inches tall and look like frozen waterfalls cascading from the plant base.
confusionNotes: With only 7 recorded observations in New England, low frostweed is easily confused with its more common cousin, Canada frostweed, which grows much taller (up to 3 feet). Remember: low stays low - if your frostweed is knee-high or taller, it's probably Canada frostweed.
contextualKnowledge: This species has recently undergone a name change in scientific circles - you may see it listed in older field guides as Crocanthemum propinquum, but it's now classified as Helianthemum propinquum, showing how plant taxonomy continues to evolve as scientists learn more.
compareHints: Low frostweed stays much shorter than Canada frostweed and has a more spreading, mat-like growth habit compared to Canada frostweed's upright stems. Unlike plains frostweed, which prefers drier prairie-like conditions, low frostweed tolerates slightly more moisture in sandy soils and has more consistently yellow flowers rather than the occasionally white-flowered plains species.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Canada frostweed can be distinguished from its frostweed relatives by its habitat preferences and size - it's typically the one you'll find in the sandiest, driest spots and tends to stay lower to the ground.
Plains frostweed is much smaller and more mat-forming than its relative Canada frostweed, which can grow up to 2 feet tall.
Bushy frostweed differs from its relatives by being the most compact and woody of New England's frostweeds.
